title: Day Trips from Gangtok: Tsomgo, Nathu La, Rumtek
meta_description: The best day trips from Gangtok: Tsomgo Lake and Baba Mandir, Nathu La, Rumtek and Lingdum, Hanuman Tok and city viewpoints, Pakyong and Aritar, with costs.
summary: From Gangtok the classic day trip is Tsomgo Lake and Baba Mandir, with Nathu La added for Indian travellers. Rumtek and Lingdum make an easy half day, and the city viewpoints fill a morning. Shared Tsomgo seats cost ₹800–1,200; a reserved SUV with Nathu La ₹5,500–7,500. Permits are needed for the high road.

sections.heading: The short answer
paras: Give Gangtok three full days and you can do the best of its day trips without rushing. One day goes to the high road: Tsomgo Lake at 3,753 m, Baba Mandir and, for Indian nationals, Nathu La at 4,310 m on the China border. One half day goes to Rumtek, the great Karma Kagyu monastery 24 km away, and Lingdum at Ranka. The other half day is for the town's own sights: Enchey, Do-drul Chorten, the Tibetology museum and the viewpoints at Ganesh Tok, Tashi and Hanuman Tok.

Order matters. Do the town and Rumtek first, at 1,500–1,650 m, and the high road second, so your body has a day or two to adjust before you climb above 4,000 m. Keep a spare day: the high road closes after snow and for army reasons, and Nathu La is commonly reported closed to tourists on Mondays and Tuesdays. Check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: Day trips at a glance
paras: Costs are indicative for 2025–26. Reserved cars carry four to six people, so splitting one is often cheaper than individual seats for a family.

rows: Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La

sections.heading: Tsomgo Lake, Baba Mandir and Nathu La
paras: The road climbs north-east out of Gangtok through forest and army camps to Tsomgo, also called Changu, a glacial lake at 3,753 m about 40 km away. The lake is sacred to the Sikkimese; it freezes for much of the winter and is ringed by rhododendrons in spring. Yaks wait by the shore for photographs and rides, and stalls sell tea, momos and hired boots. Most visitors spend an hour here.

Further on is Baba Mandir, a shrine to Sepoy Harbhajan Singh of the Punjab Regiment, who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968; army tradition holds that his spirit still guards the border. Indian nationals can continue to Nathu La, at 4,310 m, the old trade pass into Tibet's Chumbi valley, reopened to limited border trade in 2006. At the top you see the border fence, soldiers of both sides and, on clear days, the snow ranges.

All of this needs permits arranged through a registered operator, usually the afternoon before, with photo ID and two passport photos. A shared seat for Tsomgo and Baba Mandir costs ₹800–1,200; a reserved SUV with Nathu La ₹5,500–7,500. Foreigners can visit Tsomgo on a group permit but not Nathu La. Leave by 7–8 am, dress in warm layers, and come down if anyone feels unwell.

Pack for winter whatever the month: a thermal layer, a fleece, a padded or down jacket, a warm hat, gloves and shoes with grip. Snow and ice lie on the road from about December to April, and wind at Nathu La is bitter even in May. Drink water, walk slowly, and do not climb the steps at Nathu La in a rush; the air at 4,310 m holds far less oxygen than in Gangtok. Children under about five and anyone with heart or lung problems should take medical advice first, or settle for Tsomgo, which is lower.

sections.heading: Rumtek and Lingdum
paras: Rumtek, 24 km away across the Ranipool valley, is the largest monastery in Sikkim. The 16th Karmapa fled Tibet in 1959, chose the ruins of an 18th-century monastery here, and inaugurated the new Dharma Chakra Centre at Losar in 1966. A golden stupa holds his relics. Bring photo ID for the security gate, go in the morning for prayers, and walk down to the old Rumtek monastery through the village.

On the way back, stop at Lingdum, also called Ranka or Pal Zurmang Kagyud Monastery, completed in 1999, a large, bright monastery in forest about 20 km from town. A half-day taxi covering both costs ₹1,500–2,500. If you want to stay longer, Rumtek has quiet guesthouses, and a night here is calmer than Gangtok.
Dress modestly for both monasteries, remove shoes before entering the halls, walk clockwise and ask before taking photographs inside. A small donation is welcome.

sections.heading: Gangtok's own viewpoints and sights
paras: Taxi drivers sell half-day city tours by the number of 'points', and a good one is worth taking once. Start early at Tashi View Point or Ganesh Tok, a small temple on a ridge-top with a view across Gangtok, for Kanchenjunga at dawn on clear days from October to April. Hanuman Tok, a temple run by the army on a higher ridge above town, has one of the widest mountain views in Gangtok and is quiet in the early morning.

Then visit Enchey Monastery, Do-drul Chorten with its 108 prayer wheels, and the Namgyal Institute of Tibetology, usually closed on Sundays. The Himalayan Zoological Park at Bulbuley, opposite Ganesh Tok, keeps red pandas and snow leopards in large forest enclosures, a good way to see animals you will not meet in the wild. The ropeway across the town costs about ₹100–200 and gives a bird's-eye view of the ridge. End the day on MG Marg, the car-free main street, and at Lal Bazaar below it.
A reserved taxi for a half-day tour costs about ₹1,500–2,500. Agree the list of stops and the waiting time before you leave, and drop any 'points' that are just shops or souvenir stalls.

sections.heading: Longer days: Pakyong and Aritar
paras: Pakyong, 31 km south-east, is the headquarters of Pakyong district, created in 2021, and home to Sikkim's first airport, opened in 2018 on a reshaped ridge. There is not a great deal to see, but the drive through farming country is pleasant and the town is calm. It makes sense as a stop on the way to Aritar or Rongli rather than as a trip on its own.

Aritar, about 70–75 km and three hours from Gangtok near Rhenock, is a farming village at 1,400 m around Lampokhari, a long, narrow lake ringed by forest, with the Mankhim viewpoint above it. It can be done as a long day trip by reserved car for ₹4,000–5,500, but we much prefer a night in a homestay, at about ₹1,500–2,200 per person with meals, so the trip is not mostly driving. Aritar combines well with the Silk Route via Rongli.
list: Carry photo ID and passport photos for all permit trips.
Do the high road after a day or two in Gangtok.
Book shared Tsomgo seats at registered tour desks near MG Marg.
Keep a spare day for road closures and Nathu La's closed days.

sections.heading: Planning a three-day plan
paras: Day one: Tashi View Point or Hanuman Tok at dawn, Enchey for morning prayers, Do-drul Chorten and the Tibetology museum, then MG Marg in the evening. Hand your documents to a tour desk for the high-road permit. Day two: Rumtek and Lingdum in the morning, Lal Bazaar and a slow afternoon. Day three: Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and, if it is open and you are Indian, Nathu La. Swap days two and three if the weather forecast is better on day two, but keep the high road after at least one night in Gangtok.

faqs.q: What are the best day trips from Gangtok?
faqs.a: Tsomgo Lake and Baba Mandir, with Nathu La added for Indian nationals, is the classic. Rumtek and Lingdum monasteries make a relaxed half day, and the city viewpoints, Enchey, Do-drul Chorten and the Tibetology museum fill another. Aritar is better as an overnight trip than a day trip.

faqs.q: How much does a Tsomgo Lake trip cost?
faqs.a: A shared seat for Tsomgo and Baba Mandir costs about ₹800–1,200, including the permit. A reserved SUV costs about ₹4,000–5,500, or ₹5,500–7,500 with Nathu La, split among four to six people. Boots and coats hired at the roadside cost ₹100–200. Prices are indicative for 2025–26.

faqs.q: Can I visit Tsomgo and Nathu La in one day?
faqs.a: Yes, Indian nationals can visit Tsomgo Lake, Baba Mandir and Nathu La in one day trip of 8–9 hours from Gangtok, with permits arranged by a registered operator. Nathu La is commonly reported closed on Mondays and Tuesdays and after snow. Foreigners can visit Tsomgo but not Nathu La.

faqs.q: How long does the Rumtek trip take?
faqs.a: About three to four hours by reserved taxi, including an hour each way for the 24 km drive and time at the monastery. Adding Lingdum at Ranka takes about an hour more. A half-day taxi costs about ₹1,500–2,500. Carry photo ID for Rumtek's security gate.

faqs.q: Is a Gangtok city tour worth it?
faqs.a: Yes, once, if you choose the stops. Ask for Tashi View Point or Hanuman Tok, Ganesh Tok, Enchey, Do-drul Chorten, the Tibetology museum and the zoo, and skip stops that are only shops. A half-day reserved taxi costs about ₹1,500–2,500. Go early for mountain views.

Baba Mandir is a shrine on the Nathu La road to Sepoy Harbhajan Singh of the Punjab Regiment, who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968. Army tradition holds that his spirit still guards the border. Visitors stop on the Tsomgo trip; treat the shrine with respect as a place of faith.

faqs.q: Can I go to Tsomgo Lake without a permit?
faqs.a: No. Indian visitors need a permit arranged through a registered operator with photo ID and photos, usually a day ahead. Foreigners need a Protected Area Permit through a registered agency, normally in a group of two or more. You cannot drive a private outside car on the route. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which day trip suits older parents?
faqs.a: Rumtek and Lingdum, and the city viewpoints, are easy and stay at 1,500–2,000 m. Tsomgo at 3,753 m suits most healthy older travellers for a short visit. Nathu La at 4,310 m is harder; take medical advice for heart or lung conditions and turn back if anyone feels unwell.

faqs.q: Can I visit Aritar as a day trip from Gangtok?
faqs.a: You can, by reserved car for about ₹4,000–5,500, but it is about 70–75 km and three hours each way, so most of the day is driving. We prefer a night in an Aritar homestay at about ₹1,500–2,200 per person with meals, and combining it with Rongli and the Silk Route.
